## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

### 📘 PART A — Short Answer Questions (2 × 3 Marks)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam — May 2024]**
*Define a Regular Grammar. Show that the grammar $G$ with productions $S \rightarrow aS \mid bS \mid \varepsilon$ is a regular grammar. What language does it generate?*

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

A grammar $G = (V, T, P, S)$ is **regular** if every production in $P$ is either right-linear ($A \rightarrow aB$ or $A \rightarrow a$) or left-linear ($A \rightarrow Ba$ or $A \rightarrow a$).

The given productions are:
- $S \rightarrow aS$ → right-linear (terminal $a$ followed by non-terminal $S$ on the right)
- $S \rightarrow bS$ → right-linear
- $S \rightarrow \varepsilon$ → terminal-only, hence valid in both forms

Since **every** production conforms to the right-linear form, $G$ is a regular grammar. It generates $L(G) = (a+b)^*$, the set of all strings over $\{a, b\}$ including the empty string. *(Full marks: 1 for definition, 1 for verification, 1 for language identification.)*

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]**
*State two differences between a regular grammar and a context-free grammar with suitable examples.*

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| # | Regular Grammar | Context-Free Grammar |
|---|-----------------|----------------------|
| 1 | RHS has **at most one** non-terminal, and it must be at an **extreme end** (left or right). | RHS can have **any number** of non-terminals in **any position**. |
| 2 | Generates only **regular** languages (Type-3). | Generates **context-free** languages (Type-2), a strict superset. |
| 3 | Example: $S \rightarrow aS \mid b$ generates $a^*b$. | Example: $S \rightarrow aSb \mid \varepsilon$ generates $\{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\}$ — **not** regular. |
| 4 | Equivalent in power to **DFA / NFA / Regex**. | Equivalent in power to **Pushdown Automaton (PDA)**. |

---

### 📕 PART B — Long Answer Questions (Internal Choice: A or B, 14 Marks)

---

#### **QUESTION A (14 Marks)** — *[KTU University Exam — July 2024]*

**Consider the language $L = \{w \in \{a, b\}^* \mid w \text{ ends with } ab\}$.**

**(a)** Construct a right-linear grammar $G$ that generates $L$. **(7 marks)**
**(b)** Convert $G$ into an equivalent NFA and show that the string $bbab$ is accepted. **(7 marks)**

---

**Solution (a) — Grammar Construction (7 marks):**

**Step 1:** Analyze the language — strings ending in $ab$, so any prefix of $a$'s and $b$'s is allowed.

**Step 2:** Use three non-terminals to track the suffix state:
- $S$ = no relevant suffix seen
- $A$ = last symbol seen was $a$
- $B$ = last two symbols were $ab$ (accepting)

**Step 3:** Write the production set:

$$
S \rightarrow aS \mid bS \mid aA
$$

$$
A \rightarrow bB
$$

$$
B \rightarrow aA \mid bS \mid \varepsilon
$$

**Step 4:** Explanation: From $S$, we freely absorb any $a$ or $b$. When we see an $a$ that might be the start of the final $ab$, we move to $A$. From $A$, if the next symbol is $b$, we reach the accepting state $B$. From $B$, we can either terminate (epsilon) or continue reading more symbols — but if we continue, we must reset the tracking.

**Derivation of $bbab$:**

$$
S \Rightarrow bS \Rightarrow bbS \Rightarrow bbaA \Rightarrow bbabB \Rightarrow bbab
$$

✓ The grammar is right-linear and generates exactly $L$.

---

**Solution (b) — NFA Construction (7 marks):**

**Step 1:** Create states $q_S, q_A, q_B$ corresponding to $S, A, B$, plus a final state $q_F$ (which can equal $q_B$ if $q_B$ has $\varepsilon$).

**Step 2:** For each production, add a transition:

| Production | NFA Transition |
|------------|----------------|
| $S \rightarrow aS$ | $q_S \xrightarrow{a} q_S$ |
| $S \rightarrow bS$ | $q_S \xrightarrow{b} q_S$ |
| $S \rightarrow aA$ | $q_S \xrightarrow{a} q_A$ |
| $A \rightarrow bB$ | $q_A \xrightarrow{b} q_B$ |
| $B \rightarrow aA$ | $q_B \xrightarrow{a} q_A$ |
| $B \rightarrow bS$ | $q_B \xrightarrow{b} q_S$ |
| $B \rightarrow \varepsilon$ | $q_B \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} q_F$ (or $q_B$ itself is final) |

**Step 3:** Start state = $q_S$. Final state = $q_F$ (with $\varepsilon$-closure including $q_B$).

**Trace of $bbab$ on the NFA:**

$$
q_S \xrightarrow{b} q_S \xrightarrow{b} q_S \xrightarrow{a} q_A \xrightarrow{b} q_B \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} q_F
$$

✓ String $bbab$ reaches the final state and is accepted.

---

#### **QUESTION B (14 Marks)** — *[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023, Modified]*

**Consider the NFA $M = (\{p, q, r\}, \{0, 1\}, \delta, p, \{r\})$ with transitions:**
- $\delta(p, 0) = \{p, q\}$
- $\delta(p, 1) = \{p\}$
- $\delta(q, 0) = \{r\}$
- $\delta(q, 1) = \emptyset$
- $\delta(r, 0) = \emptyset$
- $\delta(r, 1) = \{r\}$

**(a)** Construct an equivalent right-linear grammar $G$ such that $L(G) = L(M)$. **(7 marks)**
**(b)** Convert the grammar obtained in (a) into a left-linear grammar. **(7 marks)**

---

**Solution (a) — NFA to Right-Linear Grammar (7 marks):**

**Step 1:** Use each state as a non-terminal: $V = \{p, q, r\}$, with start symbol $S = p$.

**Step 2:** For every transition $\delta(A, x) \ni B$, add the production $A \rightarrow xB$.

**Step 3:** For every final state $F$, add $F \rightarrow \varepsilon$.

**Productions:**

$$
p \rightarrow 0p \mid 0q \mid 1p
$$

$$
q \rightarrow 0r
$$

$$
r \rightarrow 1r \mid \varepsilon
$$

**Step 4:** Verification — derive $001$ (which should be accepted since $p \xrightarrow{0} q \xrightarrow{0} r \xrightarrow{1} r$):

$$
p \Rightarrow 0q \Rightarrow 00r \Rightarrow 001r \Rightarrow 001
$$

✓ String $001$ is in $L(M) = L(G)$.

---

**Solution (b) — Right-Linear to Left-Linear Grammar (7 marks):**

**Step 1:** Reverse all RHS strings.

**Step 2:** Swap the order of the terminal substring and the non-terminal.

**Step 3:** Apply the transformation rule: for $A \rightarrow aB$ (right-linear), produce $B \rightarrow Aa$ (left-linear). Then rename consistently.

**Standard construction (KTU 2024 procedure):**

Introduce a new start symbol $S'$ and reverse the grammar's "flow." The resulting left-linear grammar is:

$$
S' \rightarrow S
$$

$$
S \rightarrow S0 \mid S1
$$

$$
S \rightarrow Q0
$$

$$
Q \rightarrow R0
$$

$$
R \rightarrow R1 \mid \varepsilon
$$

> [!NOTE]
> The exact KTU-prescribed procedure is: (i) reverse every production's RHS, (ii) replace each $A \rightarrow xB$ with $B \rightarrow Ax$, (iii) introduce a new start symbol that produces the old start. The resulting grammar generates the **same** language.

---

### ⚠️ KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Where students commonly lose marks on Regular Grammar questions:**
> 1. **Wrong non-terminal position** — Writing $S \rightarrow aSb$ and claiming it's regular. This is **context-free**, not regular. Maximum marks deducted: **2–3 marks**.
> 2. **Forgetting $\varepsilon$ production** — When converting NFA → Grammar, students often forget to add $F \rightarrow \varepsilon$ for the final state. This causes the language to exclude the empty string. Marks lost: **1 mark**.
> 3. **Mixing left and right linear in one production set** — A grammar cannot be both. If a question asks for a right-linear grammar, ALL productions must be right-linear. Marks lost: **2 marks**.
> 4. **Not specifying all four tuple components** — Always write $G = (V, T, P, S)$ explicitly. Marks lost: **1 mark**.
> 5. **Confusing derivation with parse tree** — A regular grammar produces a **chain** (linear sequence), not a tree. Drawing a tree is technically incorrect. Marks lost: **1 mark**.

---

### 🔁 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

- ✅ A **Regular Grammar** is a 4-tuple $G = (V, T, P, S)$ where every production is **right-linear** ($A \rightarrow aB$ or $A \rightarrow a$) **or** **left-linear** ($A \rightarrow Ba$ or $A \rightarrow a$).
- ✅ The non-terminal (if present) must be at an **extreme end** of the RHS — never in the middle.
- ✅ Regular grammars generate exactly the **regular languages** — equivalent in power to DFA, NFA, and Regular Expressions.
- ✅ The grammar is the **most restrictive** (Type-3) in the Chomsky hierarchy.
- ✅ To convert **NFA → Right-Linear Grammar**: state = non-terminal, transition = production, final state → $\varepsilon$-production.
- ✅ To convert **Right-Linear → Left-Linear**: reverse all RHS strings, then re-interpret as left-linear productions.
- ✅ $\varepsilon$-productions mark a non-terminal as "accepting" — never forget them.
- ✅ Languages requiring **counting or matching** (e.g., $a^n b^n$, palindromes, balanced parentheses) are **NOT** regular — they need a **CFG / PDA**.
- ✅ The derivation of any string in a regular grammar is a **strictly linear chain** — one symbol at a time, no branching.
- ✅ For KTU exams, **always** declare the tuple $(V, T, P, S)$ explicitly, **always** justify the regularity, and **always** verify with at least one derivation trace.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCCST302 - THEORY OF COMPUTATION
> - **Module:** Module 2
> - **Topic:** Pumping Lemma as a Tool to Prove Non-Regularity of Languages

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 📘 SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Definition — The Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Pumping Lemma (Michael Sipser, 1997 — Standard KTU Formulation)**
>
> If $A$ is a **regular language**, then there exists a number $p \geq 1$ (called the *pumping length*) such that every string $s \in A$ of length at least $p$ can be written as a concatenation of three substrings $s = xyz$ satisfying the following three conditions simultaneously:
>
> 1. **Length condition (locality):** $\vert xy \vert \leq p$
> 2. **Non-triviality condition:** $\vert y \vert > 0$
> 3. **Closure under repetition (pumping):** $xy^{i}z \in A$ for every integer $i \geq 0$

The number $p$ depends *only* on the language $A$ (i.e., on the DFA/NFA that recognizes it), **not** on the chosen string $s$.

## 1.2 The Three Critical Terms

| Term | Symbol | Plain English Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Pumping Length | $p$ | A fixed constant tied to the language. Any DFA for $L$ has at most $p$ states. |
| The Pumpable Substring | $y$ | The middle piece that can be "pumped" (repeated) any number of times. |
| The Decomposition | $x, y, z$ | A split of $s$ where $x$ is the prefix, $y$ is the middle (looped in DFA), $z$ is the suffix. |

## 1.3 Conceptual Analogy — The "Replaying Music" Picture

> [!NOTE]
> **Intuition — A Cassette Tape Recorder 🎵**
>
> Imagine a finite automaton as a tiny tape recorder that has only a **finite number of buttons** (its states). When the automaton reads a long input string, the Pigeonhole Principle guarantees that *some button must be pressed twice* during the scan. The portion of the tape that plays between the first and second press of that button is the substring $y$.
>
> Now, here's the magic: because the machine ends in the *same* internal state after reading $y$ as it did after reading it once, you can loop that segment **zero, one, two, or a million times** — and the automaton will still end in an accepting state. That is precisely what "pumping" means — *replaying a loop without changing the final outcome*.
>
> If a language is regular, the machine has a finite number of states, so this "replay loop" **must** exist for long enough strings. Conversely, if you can find a string in $L$ that has *no* such replay loop, the language **cannot** be regular.

## 1.4 Why We Use It: A Tool for Proving Non-Regularity

The Pumping Lemma is a **necessary condition** for regularity — *every* regular language satisfies it, but *not every* language that satisfies it is regular. Its primary KTU-application is **proof by contradiction** to show that certain languages (e.g., $L = \{a^{n}b^{n} \mid n \geq 0\}$) are **not** regular.

## 1.5 Syllabus-Mandated Boundary Conditions

- **Required constant:** $p \geq 1$ (positive integer — the pumping length).
- **Strict inequality:** $\vert y \vert > 0$ (strictly positive; an empty $y$ is forbidden).
- **Weak inequality:** $\vert xy \vert \leq p$ (the loop must occur *within* the first $p$ characters).
- **Universal quantifier on $i$:** The pumping property must hold for **all** $i \geq 0$ (i.e., $i = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$).

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 📘 SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Why the Pumping Lemma Works — The Pigeonhole Argument

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Heart of the Theorem (Proof Sketch)**
>
> Let $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ be a DFA that recognizes $A$, and let $\vert Q \vert = p$ (number of states). Take any string $s = s_1 s_2 \dots s_n \in A$ with $n \geq p$. Consider the sequence of states traversed while reading $s$:
>
> $$q_0, q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n$$
>
> where $q_i = \delta^{*}(q_0, s_1 s_2 \dots s_i)$. This sequence contains $n+1 > p$ states, but only $p$ distinct states exist. By the **Pigeonhole Principle**, two states in this sequence must be equal: $q_i = q_j$ for some $0 \leq i < j \leq p$. The substring between positions $i+1$ and $j$ corresponds to $y$, which can be looped arbitrarily.

## 2.2 The Master Equation — Decomposition of a Pumping Candidate

For a string $s$ of length $\geq p$, the canonical decomposition is:

$$s = \underbrace{s_1 s_2 \dots s_i}_{x} \;\; \underbrace{s_{i+1} s_{i+2} \dots s_j}_{y} \;\; \underbrace{s_{j+1} \dots s_n}_{z}$$

Where the indices $i, j$ satisfy $0 \leq i < j \leq p$, giving us:
- $x = s_1 s_2 \dots s_i$
- $y = s_{i+1} \dots s_j$ with $\vert y \vert = j - i \geq 1$
- $z = s_{j+1} \dots s_n$

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Identity / Inequality | Formal Statement | Engineering Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pumping Decomposition | $s = xyz$ | A long string can be split into prefix, loop, and suffix. |
| 2 | Locality Constraint | $\vert xy \vert \leq p$ | The loop $y$ is contained within the first $p$ symbols. |
| 3 | Non-Emptiness | $\vert y \vert \geq 1$ | The loop is at least one character long. |
| 4 | Pumping Invariance | $xy^{i}z \in L \;\; \forall \, i \geq 0$ | Repeating the loop any number of times keeps us in $L$. |
| 5 | Pumping Length Bound | $p \leq \vert Q \vert$ | The pumping length is at most the number of DFA states. |
| 6 | Resulting String Length | $\vert xy^{i}z \vert = \vert s \vert + (i-1)\vert y \vert$ | Pumping grows the string by multiples of $\vert y \vert$. |
| 7 | Adversary's Choice | $s \in L$ chosen by us, decomposition forced by opponent | Proof structure is a **game**: we pick $s$, opponent picks split. |

## 2.4 The Adversarial Proof Pattern (Critical for KTU)

> [!NOTE]
> **The Three Roles in a Pumping Lemma Proof**
>
> 1. **The Mathematician (Us):** Choose a specific string $s$ of length $\geq p$.
> 2. **The Adversary (Opponent):** Chooses *any* valid split $s = xyz$ satisfying the first two conditions.
> 3. **The Mathematician (Us Again):** Picks an $i \geq 0$ such that $xy^{i}z \notin L$.
>
> Because the adversary is *free to pick the worst-case split*, our chosen $i$ must defeat **every** possible split. This is the source of the proof's strength.

## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Compiler Design:** Detects whether a language recognized by lexical analyzers (regex-based) is feasible. Non-regular patterns cannot be implemented with finite memory.
- **Network Protocol Verification:** Finite-state machines model TCP, HTTP, and BGP. The Pumping Lemma shows which protocol-level properties require unbounded buffers.
- **Digital Circuit Design:** Regular languages correspond to circuits of finite depth with feedback loops of fixed length. Non-regularity implies the need for counters/stacks.
- **Bioinformatics Pipelines:** Verifying whether DNA motif patterns can be matched with simple finite automata before deploying more complex (and expensive) pushdown automata.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 📘 SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Full Proof of the Pumping Lemma (Theorem 1.70, Sipser — KTU Standard)

> [!NOTE]
> **Theorem.** If $A$ is a regular language, then there is a number $p$ such that for every string $s \in A$ with $\vert s \vert \geq p$, we may write $s = xyz$ with (i) $\vert xy \vert \leq p$, (ii) $\vert y \vert > 0$, and (iii) $xy^{i}z \in A$ for all $i \geq 0$.

### Proof (Detailed Step-by-Step)

**Step 1 — Assume regularity.**
Let $A$ be regular. Then there exists a DFA $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ such that $L(M) = A$.

**Step 2 — Choose the pumping length.**
We define $p$ to be the number of states of $M$:
$$p \mathrel{:=} \vert Q \vert$$

> The value $p$ is a positive integer ($p \geq 1$) because any DFA has at least one state (the start state).

**Step 3 — Take an arbitrary long string.**
Let $s = s_1 s_2 \dots s_n$ be any string in $A$ with $n \geq p$. Since $M$ accepts $s$, the sequence of states traversed while reading $s$ is:
$$q_0, q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n \quad \text{where} \quad q_i = \delta^{*}(q_0, s_1 s_2 \dots s_i)$$

**Step 4 — Apply the Pigeonhole Principle.**
This sequence has $n+1$ states. Since $n \geq p$, we have $n+1 \geq p+1 > p = \vert Q \vert$. By the Pigeonhole Principle, **at least two** of these states must be identical. In particular, restricting our attention to the first $p+1$ states:
$$q_0, q_1, \dots, q_p$$

we can find indices $i, j$ with $0 \leq i < j \leq p$ such that $q_i = q_j$.

**Step 5 — Define the decomposition.**
We define:
- $x = s_1 s_2 \dots s_i$ (the prefix read before state $q_i$)
- $y = s_{i+1} s_{i+2} \dots s_j$ (the substring read transitioning from $q_i$ to $q_j$)
- $z = s_{j+1} s_{j+2} \dots s_n$ (the suffix read after state $q_j$)

By construction, $s = xyz$ as a concatenation.

**Step 6 — Verify condition (i): $\vert xy \vert \leq p$.**

$$\begin{aligned}
\vert xy \vert &= \vert x \vert + \vert y \vert \\
&= i + (j - i) \\
&= j \\
&\leq p
\end{aligned}$$

The last inequality holds because $j \leq p$ by our choice in Step 4. $\blacksquare$

**Step 7 — Verify condition (ii): $\vert y \vert > 0$.**

$$\begin{aligned}
\vert y \vert &= j - i \\
&\geq 1
\end{aligned}$$

The last inequality holds because $i < j$ (strict inequality from Step 4). $\blacksquare$

**Step 8 — Verify condition (iii): $xy^{i}z \in A$ for all $i \geq 0$.**

For any $i \geq 0$, consider the string $xy^{i}z$. We track the state trajectory:

$$\begin{aligned}
\delta^{*}(q_0, xy^{i}z) &= \delta^{*}(\delta^{*}(q_0, x), \, y^{i}z) \\
&= \delta^{*}(\delta^{*}(q_i, y^{i}), \, z) \quad \text{(since } \delta^{*}(q_0, x) = q_i\text{)} \\
&= \delta^{*}(q_i, \, z) \quad \text{(since looping } y \text{ keeps us at } q_i \text{ because } q_i = q_j\text{)} \\
&= q_n \in F
\end{aligned}$$

The state $q_n$ is the same final state the original string $s$ ends in. Since $s \in A$, we have $q_n \in F$, and therefore $xy^{i}z \in A$. $\blacksquare$

This completes the proof of the Pumping Lemma.

---

## 3.2 Application 1 — Proving $L = \{a^{n}b^{n} \mid n \geq 0\}$ is Not Regular

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Theorem.** $L = \{a^{n}b^{n} \mid n \geq 0\}$ is **not** a regular language.

### Proof by Contradiction

**Step 1 — Assume $L$ is regular.**
Suppose, for contradiction, that $L$ is regular.

**Step 2 — Apply the Pumping Lemma.**
By the Pumping Lemma, there exists a pumping length $p \geq 1$ such that every string in $L$ of length $\geq p$ can be decomposed as $s = xyz$ with $\vert xy \vert \leq p$, $\vert y \vert > 0$, and $xy^{i}z \in L$ for all $i \geq 0$.

**Step 3 — Choose the adversary's worst-case string.**
Select $s = a^{p}b^{p}$. Clearly $s \in L$ (with $n = p$) and $\vert s \vert = 2p \geq p$.

**Step 4 — Analyze the only possible split.**
Since $\vert xy \vert \leq p$ and the first $p$ characters of $s$ are all $a$'s, the substring $xy$ lies **entirely within the $a^{p}$ block**. Therefore:
- $x = a^{k}$ for some $k \geq 0$
- $y = a^{m}$ for some $m \geq 1$ (so that $\vert y \vert > 0$)
- $z = a^{p-k-m}b^{p}$ (the rest of the $a$'s followed by all the $b$'s)

**Step 5 — Pump $y$ down with $i = 0$.**
Consider the string $xy^{0}z = xz = a^{p-m}b^{p}$. This string has $p - m$ $a$'s and $p$ $b$'s. For it to be in $L = \{a^{n}b^{n}\}$, we would need:

$$p - m = p \quad \Longrightarrow \quad m = 0$$

But this contradicts $m \geq 1$ from Step 4.

**Step 6 — Conclude the contradiction.**
We have found a string $xz = a^{p-m}b^{p} \notin L$ (since $m \geq 1$), violating the Pumping Lemma. Therefore, $L$ cannot be regular. $\blacksquare$

---

## 3.3 Application 2 — Proving $L = \{ww \mid w \in \{0,1\}^{*}\}$ is Not Regular

**Step 1 — Assume $L$ is regular.**

**Step 2 — Apply the Pumping Lemma.** Pumping length $p$ exists.

**Step 3 — Choose a clever string.**
Let $s = 0^{p}1^{p}0^{p}1^{p}$. This is in $L$ (it is $ww$ with $w = 0^{p}1^{p}$), and $\vert s \vert = 4p \geq p$.

**Step 4 — Constrain the split.**
Since $\vert xy \vert \leq p$, the substring $y$ lies in the first $p$ characters of $s$, which are all $0$'s. So $y = 0^{m}$ for some $m \geq 1$.

**Step 5 — Pump up with $i = 2$.**
The string $xy^{2}z = 0^{p+m}1^{p}0^{p}1^{p}$. For this to be in $L = \{ww\}$, the string would need to be of the form $uu$ for some $u$. In particular, $\vert s' \vert = 4p + m$ would need to be even, and the first half would need to equal the second half. But the first half is $0^{p+m}1^{p}0^{p-m/2}\dots$ (a complex expression), and matching is impossible because the **pump adds extra zeros in the first block but not the second**. Formally, the number of $0$'s in the first half ($p + m + \text{some}$) cannot equal the number of $0$'s in the second half ($p$).

**Step 6 — Conclude the contradiction.** $L$ is not regular. $\blacksquare$

---

## 3.4 The Universal Pumping Lemma Proof Template (Master Recipe)

| Step | Action | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Assume $L$ is regular. | Hypothesis for proof by contradiction. |
| 2 | Pumping Lemma gives a constant $p$. | Pumping Lemma applied to the assumed DFA. |
| 3 | Choose a specific $s \in L$ with $\vert s \vert \geq p$. | Often $s = a^{p} b^{p}$ or $s = a^{p} b^{p} c^{p}$. |
| 4 | Analyze all possible $s = xyz$ with $\vert xy \vert \leq p$ and $\vert y \vert > 0$. | Use the structure of $s$ to pin down $x, y, z$. |
| 5 | Pick $i \in \{0, 2\}$ (or another) such that $xy^{i}z \notin L$. | Show the pumped string violates the definition of $L$. |
| 6 | State the contradiction. Conclude $L$ is not regular. | Formalize the negation. |

# 📘 SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 Mermaid Block Diagram — The Pumping Lemma Proof Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Start: Language L"] --> B["Assume L is Regular"]
    B --> C["Pumping Lemma Applies"]
    C --> D["Pumping Length p Exists"]
    D --> E["Choose String s in L of Length at least p"]
    E --> F["Adversary Splits s into xyz with Constraints"]
    F --> G["Constraint 1: Length of xy at most p"]
    F --> H["Constraint 2: Length of y at least 1"]
    G --> I["Try Pumping with i = 0 or i = 2"]
    H --> I
    I --> J{"Is xy Power i z Still in L?"}
    J -- Yes --> K["Contradiction Fails: Try Another i"]
    K --> I
    J -- No --> L["Found Contradiction"]
    L --> M["Conclusion: L is NOT Regular"]
    M --> N["End"]
    K -- Exhausted --> O["Adversary Picks Worst Case Split"]
    O --> F
```

**Diagram Interpretation:** This flowchart maps the adversarial proof structure. The branches where "No" is taken at the diamond (decision node) lead to a successful contradiction. The flow shows the iterative nature of the proof, where the mathematician must consider *all* possible decompositions forced by the adversary.

---

## 4.2 Mermaid Block Diagram — Anatomy of a Decomposition $s = xyz$

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph S["Input String s of length at least p"]
        X["x: Prefix"]
        Y["y: Pumpable Loop, Length at least 1"]
        Z["z: Suffix"]
    end
    X --> Y
    Y --> Z
    Y -- "Pump i = 0: Remove y" --> Y0["x concatenated with z"]
    Y -- "Pump i = 1: Original s" --> Y1["x y z"]
    Y -- "Pump i = 2: Double y" --> Y2["x y y z"]
    Y -- "Pump i = k: k Copies of y" --> YK["x y to the k z"]
```

**Diagram Interpretation:** This shows the geometric layout of the decomposition and the "pumping" operation. The loop $y$ can be deleted ($i = 0$), kept once ($i = 1$), doubled ($i = 2$), or replicated $k$ times — and the resulting string must remain in the language $L$ for the language to be regular.

---

## 4.3 Mermaid State-Transition Diagram — Pumping as a DFA Loop

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    q0["State q sub i (After reading x)"] -- "Read y once" --> q1["State q sub j (After reading y)"]
    q1 -- "Read y again (loop)" --> q1
    q1 -- "Read z (suffix)" --> qacc["State q sub n in F (Accept)"]
    q0 -- "Read z (when y is removed)" --> qacc
```

**Diagram Interpretation:** The Pumping Lemma's proof relies on the fact that the DFA, when it revisits a state while reading $y$, can loop on that state forever. Whether $y$ is read 0 times, 1 time, or 1000 times, the automaton returns to the same state $q_j = q_i$, and from there reads $z$ to reach the accepting state $q_n \in F$. This is the *only* structural reason the Pumping Lemma holds.

# 📘 SECTION 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **[KTU University Exam – May 2024]**

### **Q1. State the Pumping Lemma for regular languages. Mention all three conditions explicitly.**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**

> The Pumping Lemma states that if $A$ is a regular language, then there exists a number $p \geq 1$ (called the *pumping length*) such that every string $s \in A$ with $\vert s \vert \geq p$ can be divided into three parts $s = xyz$ satisfying:
>
> 1. $\vert xy \vert \leq p$ (the loop occurs within the first $p$ characters),
> 2. $\vert y \vert > 0$ (the loop is non-empty), and
> 3. For every $i \geq 0$, the string $xy^{i}z \in A$ (the loop can be pumped any number of times without leaving the language).

**[2 marks for the statement, 1 mark for the three conditions.]**

---

> **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**

### **Q2. What is a pumping length? How is it related to the number of states of a DFA?**

**Model Answer (3 Marks):**

> The *pumping length* $p$ of a regular language $A$ is a positive integer such that any string in $A$ of length at least $p$ can be "pumped" (i.e., has a decomposable loop) as required by the Pumping Lemma. If a DFA $M$ with $n$ states recognizes $A$, then $p \leq n$. This is because the Pigeonhole Principle guarantees a repeated state within the first $n+1$ state-transitions, and the loop between these two states gives the pumpable substring $y$.

**[1 mark for definition, 2 marks for relation to DFA states.]**

---

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — KTU ESE Module Internal Choice)

> **[KTU University Exam – May 2024 | Semester B.Tech S3 | 14 Marks]**

### **Question A**

**(a)** **[7 Marks]** State and prove the Pumping Lemma for regular languages.

**(b)** **[7 Marks]** Using the Pumping Lemma, prove that the language $L = \{a^{n}b^{n} \mid n \geq 0\}$ is not regular.

---

#### **Model Solution to Q.A(a): Statement and Proof of the Pumping Lemma**

**Statement (1 Mark):**
If $A$ is a regular language, then there exists a number $p \geq 1$ such that for every string $s \in A$ with $\vert s \vert \geq p$, we can write $s = xyz$ where:
- $\vert xy \vert \leq p$
- $\vert y \vert > 0$
- $xy^{i}z \in A$ for all $i \geq 0$

**Proof (6 Marks):**

Let $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ be a DFA recognizing $A$. Set $p = \vert Q \vert$.

Let $s = s_1 s_2 \dots s_n$ with $n \geq p$ be any string in $A$. Define $q_i = \delta^{*}(q_0, s_1 \dots s_i)$. The sequence $q_0, q_1, \dots, q_p$ has $p+1$ states but only $p$ distinct states, so by the Pigeonhole Principle there exist $0 \leq i < j \leq p$ with $q_i = q_j$.

Define:
- $x = s_1 \dots s_i$
- $y = s_{i+1} \dots s_j$
- $z = s_{j+1} \dots s_n$

**Verification of conditions:**
- $\vert xy \vert = j \leq p$ ✓
- $\vert y \vert = j - i \geq 1$ ✓
- For any $i \geq 0$, $\delta^{*}(q_0, xy^{i}z) = \delta^{*}(q_i, y^{i}z) = \delta^{*}(q_i, z) = q_n \in F$, so $xy^{i}z \in A$ ✓

∎

---

#### **Model Solution to Q.A(b): $L = \{a^{n}b^{n}\}$ is Not Regular**

**Step 1 (1 Mark):** Assume for contradiction that $L$ is regular. By the Pumping Lemma, there exists $p \geq 1$ such that every $s \in L$ with $\vert s \vert \geq p$ can be split as $s = xyz$ with the three conditions.

**Step 2 (1 Mark):** Choose $s = a^{p}b^{p}$. Clearly $s \in L$ and $\vert s \vert = 2p \geq p$.

**Step 3 (2 Marks):** Since $\vert xy \vert \leq p$ and the first $p$ characters of $s$ are all $a$'s, the substring $y$ consists entirely of $a$'s. So $y = a^{m}$ for some $m \geq 1$.

**Step 4 (2 Marks):** Consider $xy^{0}z = xz = a^{p-m}b^{p}$. For this to be in $L = \{a^{n}b^{n}\}$, we need $p - m = p$, i.e., $m = 0$, contradicting $m \geq 1$.

**Step 5 (1 Mark):** Thus $xz \notin L$, contradicting the Pumping Lemma. Therefore $L$ is not regular. ∎

---

> **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 | Semester B.Tech S3 | 14 Marks]**

### **Question B (Alternative Choice)**

**(a)** **[7 Marks]** Explain the Pumping Lemma with a suitable example. Why is it called a "Lemma" and not a "Theorem" for proving regularity?

**(b)** **[7 Marks]** Show that the language $L = \{a^{n}b^{n}c^{n} \mid n \geq 0\}$ is not regular using the Pumping Lemma.

---

#### **Model Solution to Q.B(a): Explanation of the Pumping Lemma**

**Explanation (4 Marks):**
The Pumping Lemma is a property that **every** regular language must satisfy. It states that for a regular language $L$, there exists a pumping length $p$ such that any sufficiently long string $s \in L$ contains a non-empty substring $y$ that can be repeated (pumped) arbitrarily many times while keeping the resulting string in $L$.

**Example (2 Marks):** Let $L = (ab)^{*}$. Then $p = 2$. The string $s = abab$ has length 4 ≥ 2, and we can split it as $x = \varepsilon$, $y = ab$, $z = \varepsilon$. Pumping gives $(ab)^{i}$ for all $i \geq 0$, all of which are in $L$.

**Why "Lemma" and not "Theorem" (1 Mark):**
It is a "Lemma" because it provides only a *necessary* condition for regularity, not a sufficient one. There exist non-regular languages that also satisfy the Pumping Lemma (e.g., certain non-regular languages over unary alphabases in some advanced constructions). Hence, the Pumping Lemma is a *lemma* — a helper result — used to prove non-regularity by contradiction, not a *characterization theorem* of regular languages.

---

#### **Model Solution to Q.B(b): $L = \{a^{n}b^{n}c^{n}\}$ is Not Regular**

**Step 1 (1 Mark):** Assume $L$ is regular. By the Pumping Lemma, there is a pumping length $p$.

**Step 2 (1 Mark):** Choose $s = a^{p}b^{p}c^{p}$. Then $s \in L$ and $\vert s \vert = 3p \geq p$.

**Step 3 (2 Marks):** Since $\vert xy \vert \leq p$ and the first $p$ symbols are all $a$'s, we have $y = a^{m}$ for some $m \geq 1$.

**Step 4 (2 Marks):** Consider $xy^{0}z = a^{p-m}b^{p}c^{p}$. For this to be in $L$, we would need the number of $a$'s, $b$'s, and $c$'s to be equal:
$$p - m = p = p$$
The first equality $p - m = p$ gives $m = 0$, contradicting $m \geq 1$.

**Step 5 (1 Mark):** Contradiction. Hence $L$ is not regular. ∎

---

> [!WARNING]
> **⚠️ KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls**
>
> 1. **Empty $y$ trap:** Many students write $\vert y \vert \geq 0$ instead of $\vert y \vert > 0$. This is **wrong** — condition (ii) is *strictly* greater than zero. Examiner's will deduct **1 full mark**.
>
> 2. **Confusing $p$ with string length:** Some students think $p$ is the length of the string $s$. It is *not* — $p$ is a property of the *language* (or its DFA), not of the string.
>
> 3. **Pumping the wrong way:** When proving non-regularity, students often pump *up* ($i = 2$) when pumping *down* ($i = 0$) gives a cleaner contradiction. Always check both $i = 0$ and $i = 2$ before committing.
>
> 4. **Forgetting the adversary's choice:** The Pumping Lemma proof is *adversarial* — the opponent picks the split. You must show that *no matter what split is chosen*, a contradiction arises. Showing it for *one specific* split is insufficient and loses **2–3 marks**.
>
> 5. **Mixing up $\leq$ and $\geq$:** Condition (i) is $\vert xy \vert \leq p$ (weak), but condition (ii) is $\vert y \vert > 0$ (strict). Confusing these is a common slip.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **🚀 Rapid Revision Checklist — Pumping Lemma**
>
> - ✅ The Pumping Lemma is a **necessary** (not sufficient) condition for regularity.
> - ✅ The pumping length $p$ is bounded by the number of DFA states: $p \leq \vert Q \vert$.
> - ✅ The three conditions are: $\vert xy \vert \leq p$, $\vert y \vert > 0$, $xy^{i}z \in L$ for all $i \geq 0$.
> - ✅ Proof structure is **adversarial**: we pick $s$, opponent picks split, we pick $i$.
> - ✅ Common counter-example patterns: $\{a^{n}b^{n}\}$, $\{a^{n}b^{n}c^{n}\}$, $\{ww\}$, $\{a^{n!} \}$.
> - ✅ Pump with $i = 0$ (delete $y$) or $i = 2$ (double $y$) — these are the two workhorses.
> - ✅ The Pumping Lemma **fails** for some non-regular languages — to handle those, use the **Myhill–Nerode Theorem** (covered in Module 3).
> - ✅ Remember: $x, y, z$ are **substrings** (not characters), and $x$ or $z$ may be empty, but $y$ **cannot** be empty.
> - ✅ Final exam tip: Always state the **contradiction explicitly** — do not leave the conclusion implicit.

## SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Definition of a Context-Free Grammar (CFG)

A **Context-Free Grammar (CFG)** is a formal mathematical tool used in the theory of computation to describe the syntax of programming languages and natural languages. According to the KTU 2024 Scheme syllabus for **PCCST302 – Theory of Computation**, a CFG is formally defined as a 4-tuple:

$$G = (V, \Sigma, R, S)$$

where:
- $V$ — A finite set of **variables** (also called *non-terminals* or *syntactic categories*).
- $\Sigma$ — A finite set of **terminals** (the alphabet of the language, disjoint from $V$, i.e., $V \cap \Sigma = \emptyset$).
- $R$ — A finite set of **rules** (or *productions*) of the form $A \rightarrow \alpha$, where $A \in V$ and $\alpha \in (V \cup \Sigma)^{*}$.
- $S \in V$ — A designated **start variable** from which all derivations in the grammar begin.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight — "Context-Free" Property**
> A grammar is "context-free" because the left-hand side of every production consists of a *single* non-terminal symbol. This means the rule $A \rightarrow \alpha$ can be applied *regardless of the context* in which $A$ appears in the sentential form. The right-hand side is replaced independently of its surrounding symbols.

The **language generated by a CFG** $G$, denoted $L(G)$, is the set of all strings of terminals that can be derived from the start symbol $S$:

$$L(G) = \{ w \in \Sigma^{*} \mid S \Rightarrow^{*} w \}$$

where $\Rightarrow^{*}$ denotes the reflexive-transitive closure of the derivation relation $\Rightarrow$.

---

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

> [!NOTE]
> **Plain English Analogy — The "Recipe Book" View of a CFG**
> Imagine you are a chef trying to teach a robot to cook any dish. You cannot list every possible dish (that would be infinite). Instead, you write a **recipe book** containing rules like:
> - "A *Meal* can be made from a *Main Course* followed by a *Dessert*."
> - "A *Dessert* can be an *Ice Cream* or a *Cake*."
> - "A *Cake* can be the word *chocolate-cake*."
>
> The robot starts by reading the chapter titled "**Meal**" and follows the rules step-by-step until only real food names remain. The final dish (a sequence of real food names) is what the recipe book can produce.
>
> In this analogy:
> - **Variables (V)** = Chapter titles like "Meal", "Main Course" — abstract placeholders.
> - **Terminals ($\Sigma$)** = Real food names like "chocolate-cake" — concrete, indivisible ingredients.
> - **Rules (R)** = The recipe instructions — how to expand placeholders.
> - **Start Symbol (S)** = The cover page — where the robot begins reading.
> - **The Language (L(G))** = The complete menu of all cookable dishes.

This is exactly how a CFG works. It is a *generative* system: starting from $S$, you repeatedly replace variables using the rules until only terminals remain. Any terminal string you can produce this way belongs to the language.

---

### 1.3 Why Designing CFGs is Important

In the KTU 2024 Scheme curriculum, designing CFGs bridges **abstract language theory** with **practical applications** such as:
- Defining the **syntax of programming languages** (e.g., the grammar of C, Java, Python).
- Building **compilers and parsers** (YACC, ANTLR, Bison all use CFG-based specifications).
- Modeling **structured data formats** (JSON, XML, HTML).
- Specifying **query languages** (SQL grammar, XPath).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> A well-designed CFG must be **correct** (generate *exactly* the intended language — no more, no less) and **unambiguous** where possible (each string has a unique parse tree). The design process requires creativity, pattern recognition, and rigorous mathematical verification.

## SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 The Six Canonical Strategies for Designing CFGs

Designing a CFG for a given language $L$ is fundamentally a **pattern-recognition task**. Over decades of formal language research, six recurring structural patterns have been identified that cover virtually every CFL encountered in KTU examinations. Mastering these patterns guarantees success.

#### Strategy 1: Matching / Balanced Patterns (The "$a^{n}b^{n}$" Family)
**When to use:** The language requires a *count-based relationship* between two symbols (e.g., same number of $a$'s as $b$'s, balanced parentheses, matching tags).

**Core Production Template:**
$$S \rightarrow aSb \mid \varepsilon$$

**Why it works:** The recursive rule $S \rightarrow aSb$ "stacks" an $a$ on the left and a $b$ on the right simultaneously, ensuring perfect pairing. The base case $\varepsilon$ terminates the recursion.

**Generalizations:**
- $L = \{a^{n}b^{n}c^{n} \mid n \geq 0\}$ requires *two* interdependent counters — a classic KTU 14-mark problem (see Section 5).
- $L = \{a^{i}b^{j} \mid i = 2j\}$ requires a *ratio-based* relationship.

---

#### Strategy 2: Palindromes and Symmetric Structures
**When to use:** The language consists of strings that read the same forwards and backwards, or have symmetric structure.

**Core Production Template:**
$$S \rightarrow aSa \mid bSb \mid a \mid b \mid \varepsilon$$

**Why it works:** Each recursive step adds matching symbols to *both ends*, preserving symmetry. The base cases produce single-character palindromes or the empty palindrome.

---

#### Strategy 3: Union and Concatenation
**When to use:** The language is described as a *union* of simpler languages or as a *concatenation* of structured parts.

**Core Production Template:**
$$S \rightarrow S_{1} \mid S_{2}$$
$$S \rightarrow S_{1} \, S_{2}$$

**KTU Tip:** If $L = L_{1} \cup L_{2}$, design grammars $G_{1}$ and $G_{2}$ for each piece, then add $S \rightarrow S_{1} \mid S_{2}$.

---

#### Strategy 4: Prefix/Suffix Addition
**When to use:** Every string in the language has a *fixed* prefix or suffix (or both), with a structured middle.

**Core Production Template:**
$$S \rightarrow a \, M \, b$$
where $M$ is a non-terminal generating the middle part.

---

#### Strategy 5: Kleene Star / Repetition
**When to use:** The language allows *zero or more* repetitions of a structured substring.

**Core Production Template:**
$$S \rightarrow S \, X \mid \varepsilon$$
where $X$ is the non-terminal generating the repeated structure.

**Real-world example:** $L = \{(ab)^{n} \mid n \geq 0\}$ uses $S \rightarrow aSb \mid \varepsilon$ directly, or equivalently $S \rightarrow aSb \mid \varepsilon$ viewed as repetition.

---

#### Strategy 6: Nested / Recursive Embedding
**When to use:** The language involves arbitrarily deep nesting (e.g., nested if-else, nested function calls, nested brackets).

**Core Production Template:**
$$S \rightarrow [S] \mid SS \mid \varepsilon$$
or
$$S \rightarrow (S) \mid S \, S \mid \varepsilon$$

**Why it works:** Self-reference in the production allows unlimited depth of nesting — a defining feature of context-free languages that regular languages *cannot* capture.

---

### 2.2 The CFG Design Methodology (Step-by-Step)

The KTU 2024 Scheme board examiners expect students to follow a disciplined procedure when designing CFGs. The official recommended methodology is:

1. **Analyze the language description.** Identify the *structure* of valid strings: prefixes, suffixes, balanced regions, repetition counts, nesting depths.
2. **Identify the start symbol's role.** Ask: "What is the most general form a string in $L$ can take?" This becomes $S$.
3. **Decompose recursively.** Express $S$ in terms of *simpler* non-terminals that capture the structural subcomponents.
4. **Establish base cases.** For each recursive non-terminal, define the *termination* (e.g., producing $\varepsilon$ or a single terminal).
5. **Verify completeness.** Check that the grammar generates *all* valid strings (no omissions).
6. **Verify soundness.** Check that the grammar generates *only* valid strings (no over-generation).

> [!NOTE]
> **The "Decompose and Recurse" Principle**
> Every non-terminal should represent a *meaningful sub-language*. Avoid "spaghetti grammars" where rules are invented ad-hoc. A clean CFG reflects the recursive structure of the language itself.

---

### 2.3 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

The following table summarizes every essential component, notation, and verification rule you must memorize for KTU examinations.

| **Concept** | **Formal Symbol / Formula** | **Meaning / Use** | **KTU Frequency** |
|:------------|:---------------------------|:------------------|:------------------|
| CFG 4-Tuple | $G = (V, \Sigma, R, S)$ | Full grammar definition | Very High |
| Production Rule | $A \rightarrow \alpha$ | $A$ generates $\alpha$ in one step | Very High |
| Derivation Step | $uAv \Rightarrow u\alpha v$ | One rule application | High |
| Reflexive-Transitive Closure | $S \Rightarrow^{*} w$ | Zero or more derivation steps | Very High |
| Generated Language | $L(G) = \{w \in \Sigma^{*} \mid S \Rightarrow^{*} w\}$ | All terminal strings derivable from $S$ | Very High |
| Disjointness Constraint | $V \cap \Sigma = \emptyset$ | Variables and terminals never overlap | High |
| $\varepsilon$-Production | $A \rightarrow \varepsilon$ | Produces empty string (must be explicit) | High |
| Unit Production | $A \rightarrow B$ (where $B \in V$) | Single-variable on RHS — should be eliminated | Medium |
| Useless Production | $A \rightarrow \alpha$ unreachable or non-terminating | Must be removed in simplification | Medium |
| Left Recursion | $A \rightarrow A\alpha$ | Causes top-down parser issues | Medium |
| Ambiguity Indicator | Two distinct parse trees for one string | $G$ is ambiguous if such a string exists | High |

| Greibach Normal Form | $A \rightarrow a\alpha$ | RHS begins with a terminal | Medium |
| Pumping Lemma for CFL | $\vert uvxyz \vert \leq p$, $\vert vx \vert \geq 1$, $uv^{i}xy^{i}z \in L$ | Proves a language is *not* context-free | High |
| Closure under Union | $L_{1}, L_{2}$ CFL $\Rightarrow L_{1} \cup L_{2}$ CFL | Constructive: combine start symbols | High |
| Closure under Concatenation | $L_{1}, L_{2}$ CFL $\Rightarrow L_{1}L_{2}$ CFL | New start with two branches | High |
| Closure under Kleene Star | $L$ CFL $\Rightarrow L^{*}$ CFL | Recursive start production | High |
| *Not* Closed under Intersection | $L_{1} \cap L_{2}$ may not be CFL | Use pumping lemma to detect | High |
| *Not* Closed under Complement | $\overline{L_{1}}$ may not be CFL | Same as above | Medium |

### 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

The CFG design patterns are not merely academic exercises. In professional software engineering:

- **Compiler Construction:** Tools like **YACC (Yet Another Compiler Compiler)** and **ANTLR** take a CFG as input and automatically generate a parser. The CFG must be unambiguous and typically in LALR(1) or LL(1) form for practical use.
- **Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs):** SQL, HTML, JSON, and YAML are all formally specified by CFGs (or closely related formalisms).
- **Static Analysis:** Linters, formatters, and refactoring tools rely on CFG-based AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) representations.
- **Bioinformatics:** CFGs model **RNA secondary structure**, **protein folding patterns**, and **DNA sequence motifs**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Industrial Perspective Note**
> The ability to design a *minimal, unambiguous* CFG is a core competency tested in KTU's Outcome-Based Education (OBE) framework, specifically mapped to Course Outcome **CO2**: "Design context-free grammars for formal languages and analyze their properties."

## SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

This section demonstrates the *complete, exhaustive* design process for several KTU-frequently-tested languages. Every algebraic transition is explicitly explained.

---

### Example 1: $L = \{a^{n}b^{n} \mid n \geq 1\}$ (The Canonical Matching Language)

**Language Description:** All strings consisting of one or more $a$'s followed by an equal number of $b$'s.

#### Step 1 — Analyze the Structure
A valid string has the form $a \ldots a \, b \ldots b$ with the count of $a$'s exactly matching the count of $b$'s. Examples: $ab$, $aabb$, $aaabbb$, $aaaa\ldots bbbb\ldots$.

#### Step 2 — Identify the Recursive Decomposition
The most general valid string is "$a$, followed by a string of one fewer $a$'s-and-$b$'s, followed by $b$":
$$S \Rightarrow a \, S' \, b$$
where $S'$ generates the same language but with the count reduced by 1. So $S' = S$ itself.

#### Step 3 — Write the Recursive Production
$$S \rightarrow aSb$$

#### Step 4 — Establish the Base Case
The smallest valid string is $ab$ (when $n = 1$). So we need a rule that produces $ab$ directly:
$$S \rightarrow ab$$

#### Step 5 — Final Grammar
$$G = (\{S\}, \{a, b\}, \{S \rightarrow aSb \mid ab\}, S)$$

#### Step 6 — Verification by Derivation (Exhaustive)

Derivation of $aaabbb$ (the case $n = 3$):

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &\Rightarrow aSb &&\text{(Step 1: apply } S \rightarrow aSb) \\
  &\Rightarrow aaSbb &&\text{(Step 2: apply } S \rightarrow aSb \text{ to inner } S) \\
  &\Rightarrow aaaSbbb &&\text{(Step 3: apply } S \rightarrow aSb \text{ to inner } S) \\
  &\Rightarrow aaa \, ab \, bbb &&\text{(Step 4: apply } S \rightarrow ab \text{ to inner } S) \\
  &\Rightarrow aaabbb &&\text{(Step 5: concatenate terminals)}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Completeness Check:** For any $n \geq 1$, after exactly $(n-1)$ applications of $S \rightarrow aSb$ and one application of $S \rightarrow ab$, we obtain $a^{n}b^{n}$. ✓

**Soundness Check:** Every derivation produces a string of the form $a^{k}b^{k}$ for some $k \geq 1$. No other string can be produced. ✓

---

### Example 2: $L = \{a^{n}b^{n}c^{n} \mid n \geq 0\}$ (Triple Matching — KTU Classic)

**Language Description:** Equal counts of $a$, $b$, and $c$ in that order.

#### Step 1 — Recognize the Difficulty
This language is *not* context-free in a single-rule recursion. A regular CFG cannot enforce two *independent* equalities ($a$'s = $b$'s AND $b$'s = $c$'s). However, $a^{n}b^{n}c^{n}$ *is* context-free — it requires a *coordinated* recursion.

#### Step 2 — Decompose into Two Synchronized Recursions
The key insight: generate $a$'s and $c$'s *simultaneously* on the outside, with $b$'s accumulating in the middle.

Introduce an auxiliary non-terminal $A$ to handle the inner $b$'s:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &\rightarrow aSc \mid A \\
A &\rightarrow bAc \mid bc
\end{aligned}
$$

#### Step 3 — Step-by-Step Derivation of $aabbcc$ (n = 2)

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &\Rightarrow aSc &&\text{(Step 1: apply } S \rightarrow aSc) \\
  &\Rightarrow aAc &&\text{(Step 2: apply } S \rightarrow A \text{ to inner } S) \\
  &\Rightarrow abAcc &&\text{(Step 3: apply } A \rightarrow bAc) \\
  &\Rightarrow abbAcc &&\text{(Step 4: apply } A \rightarrow bAc) \\
  &\Rightarrow abbc \cdot cc &&\text{(Step 5: apply } A \rightarrow bc) \\
  &\Rightarrow aabbcc &&\text{(Step 6: concatenate)}
\end{aligned}
$$

#### Step 4 — Verification
- Each application of $S \rightarrow aSc$ adds one $a$ to the left and one $c$ to the right, but does *not* yet generate $b$'s.
- The $A$ non-terminal then generates an equal number of $b$'s and $c$'s in the middle, with the outer $c$'s being the *cumulative* result of both $S$ and $A$ recursions.
- This coordinated approach ensures all three counts match. ✓

---

### Example 3: $L = \{ww^{R} \mid w \in \{a, b\}^{*}\}$ (Even-Length Palindromes)

**Language Description:** Strings of even length that read the same forwards and backwards.

#### Step 1 — Structural Analysis
A palindrome has matching outer characters. The empty string $\varepsilon$ is a palindrome, and single characters are palindromes, but for *even-length* palindromes, the structure is "outer-matching pair wrapping an even palindrome."

#### Step 2 — Design the Grammar

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &\rightarrow aSa \mid bSb \mid aa \mid bb \mid \varepsilon
\end{aligned}
$$

#### Step 3 — Derivation of $abba$ (where $w = ab$, $w^{R} = ba$)

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &\Rightarrow aSa &&\text{(Step 1: apply } S \rightarrow aSa) \\
  &\Rightarrow abSba &&\text{(Step 2: apply } S \rightarrow bSb \text{ to inner } S) \\
  &\Rightarrow ab \, \varepsilon \, ba &&\text{(Step 3: apply } S \rightarrow \varepsilon) \\
  &\Rightarrow abba &&\text{(Step 4: concatenate)}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

### Example 4: $L = \{a^{i}b^{j}c^{k} \mid i + j = k\}$ (Arithmetic Constraint)

**Language Description:** The number of $c$'s equals the sum of the number of $a$'s and $b$'s.

#### Step 1 — Strategy
We need to generate $c$'s in two waves: one $c$ for each $a$, and one $c$ for each $b$. Use a non-terminal that produces $a$'s and $c$'s in pairs first, then $b$'s and $c$'s in pairs.

#### Step 2 — Grammar Design

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &\rightarrow AC \\
A &\rightarrow aAc \mid \varepsilon \\
C &\rightarrow bCc \mid \varepsilon
\end{aligned}
$$

#### Step 3 — Derivation of $aabccc$ (where $i=2, j=1, k=3$)

$$
\begin{aligned}
S &\Rightarrow AC &&\text{(Step 1: apply } S \rightarrow AC) \\
  &\Rightarrow aAc \cdot C &&\text{(Step 2: apply } A \rightarrow aAc) \\
  &\Rightarrow aaAcc \cdot C &&\text{(Step 3: apply } A \rightarrow aAc) \\
  &\Rightarrow aacc \cdot C &&\text{(Step 4: apply } A \rightarrow \varepsilon) \\
  &\Rightarrow aacc \cdot bCc &&\text{(Step 5: apply } C \rightarrow bCc) \\
  &\Rightarrow aacc \cdot bcc &&\text{(Step 6: apply } C \rightarrow \varepsilon) \\
  &\Rightarrow aabccc &&\text{(Step 7: concatenate)}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

### Example 5: $L = \{w \in \{0, 1\}^{*} \mid w \text{ has an equal number of 0's and 1's}\}$ (Unconstrained Counting)

**Language Description:** Binary strings with $\#0 = \#1$ (no positional restriction).

#### Step 1 — Recognize the Limitation
This language is *not* context-free. We can prove this using the **Pumping Lemma for CFLs**. Any attempt to design a CFG will fail — the grammar would need to "remember" two independent counts across arbitrary interleavings.

#### Step 2 — Why No CFG Exists (Pumping Lemma Sketch)
Assume a CFG exists with pumping length $p$. Consider the string $s = 0^{p}1^{p}0^{p}1^{p}$, which is in $L$ (each symbol appears $2p$ times — wait, that means $p+p$ each, so equal).

By the Pumping Lemma, $s = uvxyz$ with $\vert uvxyz \vert \leq p$ and $\vert vx \vert \geq 1$. Pumping *down* to $uv^{0}xy^{0}z$ would alter the count of one symbol type without compensating, breaking the equality. Hence no CFG exists.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **This is a classic KTU "trick question."** Students often try to design a CFG for this language and lose marks because they fail to recognize it is *not* context-free. Always check the pumping lemma constraint before committing to a grammar design.

### 4.3 Mermaid Diagram: Grammar Architecture for $a^{n}b^{n}c^{n}$

This block diagram shows the *division of labor* between the non-terminals $S$ and $A$ in the triple-matching grammar.

```mermaid

        S_Start[S Start Symbol] -->|aSc| S_Rec[Recursive Call]

    end
```

**Functional Insight:**
- $S$ manages the *outer shell* of $a$'s and $c$'s.
- $A$ manages the *inner region* of $b$'s and the *remaining* $c$'s.
- The two recursions are *coordinated* through the production $S \rightarrow A$ (the base case of $S$).
